title: Fairness, Accountability and Society
subtitle: Sources of harm, documentation, practitioners, audits, LLM risks
overview: This stage covers where algorithmic harms come from, how documentation and audits create accountability, what practitioners struggle with, how users expose problems, and the risks of LLMs, including their power to change beliefs. It widens HAI research from one user to everyone AI affects.

modules.title: Where harms come from
modules.goal: Use concrete cases to explain how bias enters ML through data, labels, and evaluation, and name the main sources of harm.
modules.guide: Start with Gender Shades (who is missing from the benchmark?) and Obermeyer et al. (what does the label measure?). Then use Suresh & Guttag to place each in the ML pipeline. For the math, read Barocas, Hardt & Narayanan's classification chapter (optional). Key terms: 'benchmark' (standard test set); 'intersectional' (attribute combinations); 'proxy label' (measurable stand-in, e.g., cost for need); 'representation bias' (under-sampled groups); 'measurement bias' (uneven measurement across groups).

resources.title: Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification
resources.why: Shows large accuracy gaps for darker-skinned women in commercial systems, gaps that standard benchmarks hid.
resources.focus: Read how the Pilot Parliaments Benchmark was built, Fitzpatrick skin typing, and intersectional error results.

resources.title: Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations
resources.why: A clear real-world case of label choice bias: predicting cost instead of need created racial disparities in care.
resources.focus: Read the whole paper, especially how same-score patients differed in health needs, and the reformulated label.

resources.title: A Framework for Understanding Sources of Harm throughout the Machine Learning Life Cycle
resources.why: Replaces the vague phrase 'biased data' with seven distinct sources of harm, each with its own mitigation.
resources.focus: Read the life-cycle figure and the definition and example for each of the seven sources.

resources.title: Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities
resources.why: The standard free textbook on algorithmic fairness, and the formal companion to these case studies.
resources.focus: Read the introduction and the classification chapter (independence, separation, sufficiency, and why they conflict).

quiz.q: In Gender Shades, which group had the highest error rates across the commercial gender classifiers?
quiz.explain: Darker-skinned females were the most misclassified group (error rates up to about 35%), while lighter-skinned males had error rates under 1%.

quiz.q: Why did Buolamwini & Gebru build a new benchmark (the Pilot Parliaments Benchmark)?
choices: Existing benchmarks were too small to train models
They wanted to test speech recognition
Existing face benchmarks were overwhelmingly lighter-skinned, so aggregate accuracy hid poor performance on darker-skinned groups
quiz.explain: They found common benchmarks were dominated by lighter-skinned subjects, and built a benchmark balanced by skin type and gender to enable intersectional evaluation.

quiz.q: According to Obermeyer et al., why did the health algorithm underestimate Black patients' needs?
choices: It predicted health costs as a proxy for health needs, and less money is spent on Black patients with the same level of need
It used race as an input feature
It was trained on too little data
quiz.explain: The bias came from the label: cost is not equal to need across groups. Reformulating the target so it no longer used cost as a proxy for need eliminated the bias in predicting who needs extra care.

quiz.q: Which of Suresh & Guttag's sources of harm best describes the Obermeyer et al. case?
choices: Measurement bias: the chosen label (cost) measures the target concept (need) unevenly across groups
quiz.explain: Measurement bias arises when features or labels are poor or uneven proxies for the construct of interest. Using cost to stand in for need is a classic example.

quiz.q: Which Suresh & Guttag source of harm best describes Gender Shades' finding that common benchmarks under-represented darker-skinned people?
choices: Evaluation bias: the benchmark used to judge performance does not represent the population the model will serve
quiz.explain: Evaluation bias occurs when benchmark data do not represent the use population, so good benchmark scores hide subgroup failures. (Unrepresentative training data would be representation bias.)

quiz.q: Why do Suresh & Guttag argue it is useful to name distinct sources of harm instead of saying 'the data is biased'?
choices: Because each source points to different, more targeted mitigations and allows more precise communication
Because data is never the problem
quiz.explain: The framework aims at more productive communication and application-grounded mitigation: collecting more data fixes representation bias but not historical or measurement bias.

quiz.q: In the Barocas, Hardt & Narayanan textbook, what are independence, separation, and sufficiency?
choices: Three formal group-fairness criteria for classifiers that, in general, cannot all be satisfied at once
quiz.explain: The classification chapter formalizes these criteria and shows that, except in degenerate cases, they conflict, so choosing among them is a value judgment.

modules.exercise: Choose a deployed AI system you know (e.g., resume screening). For each of Suresh & Guttag's seven sources of harm, write one sentence on how it could appear in that system, then pick the two most likely and describe an audit study (data, comparison groups, metric) that would detect each.

modules.title: Documentation and accountability
modules.goal: Describe what model cards, datasheets, and internal audit frameworks document, and explain how documentation supports accountability.
modules.guide: Read Datasheets for Datasets and Model Cards together, companion proposals for data and models. Both are lists of questions: who answers them, and who reads them? Then read Raji et al., which extends documentation into an internal audit process. Key terms: 'intended use' (contexts a model was designed for); 'disaggregated evaluation' (per-subgroup performance); 'accountability' (answering to someone who can respond); 'internal audit' (by the developer, not outsiders).

resources.title: Datasheets for Datasets
resources.authors: Gebru, Morgenstern, Vecchione, Wortman Vaughan, Wallach, Daumé, Crawford
resources.why: The standard proposal for dataset documentation; its questions are now used across industry and research.
resources.focus: Read the electronics datasheet analogy and skim the questions, organized by dataset life cycle.

resources.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
resources.authors: Mitchell, Wu, Zaldivar, Barnes, Vasserman, Hutchinson, Spitzer, Raji, Gebru
resources.why: Defines the model card, now a common release format, built around intended use and disaggregated evaluation.
resources.focus: Read the list of model card sections and the two example cards (smiling detection, toxicity).

resources.title: Closing the AI Accountability Gap: Defining an End-to-End Framework for Internal Algorithmic Auditing
resources.authors: Raji, Smart, White, Mitchell, Gebru, Hutchinson, Smith-Loud, Theron, Barnes
resources.why: Turns documentation into an organizational audit process, borrowing audit practices from other high-stakes industries.
resources.focus: Read the motivation, the SMACTR framework stages, and the documents produced at each stage.

quiz.q: What analogy motivates Datasheets for Datasets?
choices: Datasheets that accompany every electronic component, describing operating characteristics, test results, and recommended uses
quiz.explain: Gebru et al. propose that, like electronic components, every dataset should come with a datasheet documenting motivation, composition, collection, recommended uses, and more.

quiz.q: Which communication gap do datasheets mainly aim to close?
choices: Between dataset creators and dataset consumers
Between end users and app stores
quiz.explain: Datasheets are meant to improve communication between those who create datasets and those who use them, and to push the field toward transparency and accountability.

quiz.q: What is a central feature of a model card's evaluation section?
choices: Performance benchmarked across relevant groups, including intersectional groups, relevant to the intended use
quiz.explain: Model cards report disaggregated evaluation across cultural, demographic, or phenotypic groups and their intersections, along with intended use and evaluation details.

quiz.q: Why do model cards emphasize documenting the intended use of a model?
choices: To discourage use in contexts the model is not suited for
To make the model run faster
quiz.explain: Mitchell et al. aim to clarify intended use cases and minimize use in unsuitable contexts; performance claims only hold for the conditions evaluated.

quiz.q: What gap does Raji et al.'s internal audit framework address?
choices: It is hard for organizations to identify harms of their own systems before deployment, and emergent issues afterward are hard to trace back to their source
The lack of GPUs for auditing
Models are too accurate to audit
quiz.explain: Most audits are external and after deployment. SMACTR embeds auditing throughout internal development, with each stage producing documents that form an audit report.

quiz.q: A company publishes a polished model card but nobody inside the company has to act on what it reports. Which idea from Raji et al. does this most clearly lack?
choices: A process that ties documentation to the organization's stated values and decisions throughout development
quiz.explain: Raji et al. argue documentation must be part of an end-to-end process that assesses decisions against the organization's principles; a document alone does not create accountability.

modules.exercise: Find a real model card or dataset card on a public model hub. Score it against the sections proposed by Mitchell et al. or Gebru et al.: which are missing or vague? Then write two questions a downstream user would need answered before deploying it in a hospital, and say which proposed section should have answered them.

modules.title: Practitioners and data work
modules.goal: Explain what practitioners need to build fairer systems, why data work is undervalued, and how choosing whose labels count shapes models.
modules.guide: Start with Holstein et al., comparing practitioners' needs with what fairness research offers. Then Sambasivan et al. introduce 'data cascades' from interviews in several countries. Gordon et al. (optional) make labeling's social choice explicit. Key terms: 'semi-structured interview' (planned questions plus follow-ups); 'data cascade' (compounding problems from data issues); 'ground truth' (labels treated as correct); 'annotator disagreement' (labelers differ, often by group); 'majority vote' (default aggregation that can override minorities).

resources.title: Improving fairness in machine learning systems: What do industry practitioners need?
resources.authors: Holstein, Wortman Vaughan, Daumé, Dudík, Wallach
resources.why: The first systematic study of practitioners' fairness needs, showing where research tools miss real practice.
resources.focus: Read the method (35 interviews, 267 survey respondents) and findings on data collection, auditing, research gaps.

resources.title: “Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work”: Data Cascades in High-Stakes AI
resources.authors: Sambasivan, Kapania, Highfill, Akrong, Paritosh, Aroyo
resources.why: Names and documents data cascades: how undervalued data work causes serious failures in high-stakes AI.
resources.focus: Read the data cascade definition, cascade types and triggers, and the HCI opportunities in the discussion.

resources.title: Jury Learning: Integrating Dissenting Voices into Machine Learning Models
resources.authors: Gordon, Lam, Park, Patel, Hancock, Hashimoto, Bernstein
resources.why: Exposes a hidden choice in supervised learning, whose labels count, and lets practitioners make it deliberately.
resources.focus: Read the motivation (majority vote overrides minority groups) and the jury metaphor; skim the architecture.

quiz.q: What methods did Holstein et al. use to study practitioners' fairness needs?
choices: 35 semi-structured interviews and an anonymous survey of 267 ML practitioners
quiz.explain: They combined interviews and a survey of commercial product teams to identify alignment and disconnect between practitioners' challenges and fair-ML research.

quiz.q: Which mismatch between fairness research and practice does Holstein et al.'s study highlight?
choices: Research focused largely on algorithmic fixes to a fixed dataset, while practitioners often wanted support earlier in the pipeline, such as collecting and curating data
Research tools were too easy to use
quiz.explain: Practitioners often could influence data collection and wanted help there, and frequently lacked the demographic information many fairness tools assume.

quiz.q: What is a 'data cascade' according to Sambasivan et al.?
choices: A type of neural network layer
Compounding events that cause negative downstream effects from data issues
quiz.explain: Data cascades are triggered by practices that undervalue data quality; they are pervasive (92% of the 53 practitioners interviewed), invisible, delayed, and often avoidable.

quiz.q: Why are data cascades especially dangerous in the high-stakes domains Sambasivan et al. studied?
choices: Because they are always caught immediately
Because they only affect training speed
Because they are often invisible and delayed, so problems surface after deployment in areas like health or conservation where errors matter most
Because high-stakes models never use data
quiz.explain: Cascades are hard to see and appear late, and in high-stakes AI the downstream impact of poor data quality is magnified.

quiz.q: What problem with standard supervised learning does Jury Learning address?
choices: Label disagreements are resolved implicitly by majority vote, which overrides minority groups' labels
quiz.explain: Gordon et al. make the choice explicit: practitioners specify which people or groups, in what proportions, form the 'jury' whose modeled labels determine predictions.

quiz.q: How do Sambasivan et al. and Holstein et al. reach a similar conclusion from different angles?
choices: Both find that practitioners' real difficulties lie heavily in data (collection, quality, documentation) rather than only in model design
Both say fairness is solved by better algorithms
quiz.explain: Holstein et al. find practitioners want help with data collection and curation; Sambasivan et al. show undervalued data work causes cascades. Both argue for treating data as first-class.

modules.exercise: Draft an interview guide (8-10 questions) for practitioners building an LLM content-moderation system, aiming to uncover data cascades and annotator disagreement. Mark which questions draw on Sambasivan et al. and which on Gordon et al., and describe how you would recruit a sample that avoids studying only large tech companies.

modules.title: Everyday users and algorithm audits
modules.goal: Describe how people reason about invisible algorithms, how algorithm audits are designed, and how everyday users collectively surface harmful behavior.
modules.guide: Start with Eslami et al.: a daily-use feed algorithm can be invisible, and revealing it changes reactions. Then Sandvig et al. map audit designs borrowed from discrimination research. Finish with Shen et al. on users as auditors. Key terms: 'algorithmic awareness' (knowing an algorithm curates content); 'audit study' (testing outputs for discrimination); 'sock puppet' (fake test account); 'scraping' (automated output collection); 'everyday algorithm auditing' (users surfacing harms in normal use).

resources.title: "I always assumed that I wasn't really that close to [her]": Reasoning about Invisible Algorithms in News Feeds
resources.authors: Eslami, Rickman, Vaccaro, Aleyasen, Vuong, Karahalios, Hamilton, Sandvig
resources.why: Shows that many daily users did not know their feed was curated, and learning this changed their reactions.
resources.focus: Read the FeedVis tool description, the awareness finding, and the follow-up with participants months later.

resources.title: Auditing Algorithms: Research Methods for Detecting Discrimination on Internet Platforms
resources.why: The classic taxonomy of algorithm audit designs, with their strengths and their legal and ethical problems.
resources.focus: Read the history of audit studies and the five audit designs; note terms-of-service and legal risks.

resources.title: Everyday algorithm auditing: Understanding the power of everyday users in surfacing harmful algorithmic behaviors
resources.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
resources.why: Defines everyday algorithm auditing and argues users catch harms formal audits miss, with implications for platform design.
resources.focus: Read the definition, the real-world case analysis, and design implications for tools supporting user audits.

quiz.q: What was a key finding of Eslami et al.'s study of Facebook News Feed users?
choices: More than half of participants were not aware that the News Feed was curated by an algorithm
All participants knew exactly how the feed algorithm worked
Participants preferred an unfiltered feed and quit Facebook
The algorithm showed every post from every friend
quiz.explain: Using FeedVis to compare curated and unfiltered feeds, the study found most participants were initially unaware of curation, and some had drawn wrong conclusions about friendships from what they saw.

quiz.q: Why does the title quote ('I always assumed that I wasn't really that close to [her]') matter for HAI?
choices: It shows users blame themselves or others for outcomes actually caused by an invisible algorithm
It shows users always understand algorithms
It shows users dislike their friends
It shows the algorithm was perfectly accurate
quiz.explain: Without awareness of curation, users explained missing posts through social reasons. Invisible algorithms shape beliefs about relationships, not just about content.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the audit designs described by Sandvig et al.?
quiz.explain: Sandvig et al. describe code audits, noninvasive user audits, scraping audits, sock puppet audits, and crowdsourced (collaborative) audits. 'Federated gradient audit' is invented.

quiz.q: What is a key drawback Sandvig et al. raise for scraping and sock puppet audits?
choices: They are impossible to run on the internet
They can violate platforms' terms of service and raise legal risk for researchers
They require access to the platform's source code
quiz.explain: These designs collect data or create fake accounts in ways platforms may prohibit, which Sandvig et al. discuss as a legal and ethical obstacle to auditing.

quiz.q: What do Shen et al. claim about everyday users as auditors?
choices: Users can only audit if they understand the underlying algorithm
Formal audits make user audits unnecessary
Users can surface problematic machine behaviors that elude centrally organized audits, regardless of their knowledge of the algorithm
quiz.explain: Everyday algorithm auditing happens through day-to-day use; because it is grounded in real contexts, it can catch issues formal audits miss, even without technical knowledge.

quiz.q: Which design implication follows most directly from Shen et al.?
choices: Platforms should hide algorithmic outputs from users
Platforms and tools could support users in detecting, discussing, and reporting problematic behavior, and connect user findings with formal audits
Audits should happen once before launch
quiz.explain: Shen et al. draw lessons for designing platforms and tools that facilitate everyday auditing and bridge it with formal auditing approaches.

modules.exercise: Pick one of Sandvig et al.'s audit designs and plan an audit of an LLM chatbot for differential treatment by user dialect. Specify the inputs you would vary, what you would hold constant, the outcome measure, how many samples you need to account for randomness in generation, and one legal or ethical issue you would need to resolve.

modules.title: Risks of language models
modules.goal: Map the main categories of LLM risk, explain the 'stochastic parrots' critique, and evaluate evidence that AI dialogue can durably change beliefs.
modules.guide: Read Bender et al. first, a short critique of environmental, data, and meaning-related problems. Then map risks with Weidinger et al., noting HCI harms. Finish with Costello et al., where GPT-4 dialogues durably reduced conspiracy beliefs; what does that imply about manipulation risk? Key terms: 'stochastic parrot' (word patterns without meaning); 'information hazard' (harm from revealing true information); 'anthropomorphism' (attributing human qualities to systems); 'durable effect' (lasting weeks or months).

resources.title: On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?
resources.why: A widely cited critique of large language models, central to debates about scale, data, and meaning.
resources.focus: Read the sections on environmental and financial costs, undocumentable training data, 'stochastic parrots', and the recommendations.

resources.title: Ethical and social risks of harm from Language Models
resources.authors: Weidinger, Mellor, Rauh, Griffin, Uesato, et al.
resources.why: A widely used taxonomy of LM risks (six areas, 21 risks) underlying many evaluation and policy efforts.
resources.focus: Read the six-area summary and the Human-Computer Interaction Harms section in full; skim the others.

resources.title: Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI
resources.why: Experimental evidence that personalized AI dialogue can change entrenched beliefs, relevant to both beneficial uses and manipulation.
resources.focus: Read the GPT-4 Turbo dialogue design, effect size, two-month follow-up, and spillover to unrelated conspiracies.

quiz.q: What does Bender et al.'s phrase 'stochastic parrot' describe?
choices: A model that understands meaning but speaks randomly
A robot that imitates bird calls
A system that strings words together according to statistical patterns of how they co-occur, with no grasp of what they mean
A model trained only on small datasets
quiz.explain: The metaphor warns that fluent output can mislead people into attributing understanding and intent to a system that models form, not meaning.

quiz.q: Which of these is one of Bender et al.'s recommendations?
choices: Scale models as fast as possible
Invest in curating and carefully documenting datasets rather than ingesting everything on the web
quiz.explain: They recommend weighing environmental and financial costs first, curating and documenting data, pre-development exercises tied to stakeholder values, and research beyond ever-larger models.

quiz.q: Which risk area in Weidinger et al. covers risks specific to conversational agents interacting with users, such as unsafe use, manipulation, or deception?
quiz.explain: The HCI Harms area focuses on LLM-based conversational agents, including users overtrusting or anthropomorphizing them, and manipulation or deception.

quiz.q: In Weidinger et al.'s taxonomy, a model correctly inferring a user's sensitive health condition from their writing falls under which area?
quiz.explain: Information hazards include private data leaks and LMs correctly inferring sensitive information; the harm comes from true information.

quiz.q: What did Costello, Pennycook & Rand find?
choices: AI dialogues had no effect on conspiracy beliefs
Personalized evidence-based dialogues with GPT-4 Turbo reduced conspiracy belief by about 20%, and the effect remained two months later
The effect disappeared within a day
Only people with weak beliefs changed
quiz.explain: The reduction persisted at two months, generalized across conspiracy theories, occurred even among deeply entrenched believers, and spilled over to unrelated conspiracies.

quiz.q: What theoretical claim does the Costello et al. result challenge?
choices: That people never change their minds
That conspiracy beliefs resist counterevidence because they fulfill psychological needs; the results suggest past failures may reflect counterevidence that was not compelling or tailored enough
quiz.explain: Influential accounts say such beliefs resist evidence because they meet psychological needs. Costello et al. suggest many believers update when evidence is sufficiently compelling and tailored.

quiz.q: Connecting Costello et al. and Jakesch et al. (Stage 8), what is the most defensible conclusion?
choices: LLMs can shift people's beliefs through interaction, so the same capability that corrects misinformation could steer opinions in unintended or harmful directions
quiz.explain: Jakesch et al. found opinionated suggestions shifted attitudes; Costello et al. found targeted dialogue reduced conspiracy belief. Together they show influence is a capability, which is why Weidinger et al. list manipulation as an HCI harm.

modules.exercise: Costello et al. used AI dialogue to reduce false beliefs. Write a short research ethics memo (half a page) for a team that wants to use the same method to increase vaccine uptake. Address consent, which beliefs count as 'false' and who decides, how you would detect if the model itself states false information, and one risk from Weidinger et al.'s taxonomy.
